title: Know, then Draw: A New Learning Paradigm for Visual Generation

paper.title: Know, then Draw: A New Learning Paradigm for Visual Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Visual generation requires both high-level semantic knowledge and fine-grained
pixel details. We propose a learning paradigm that assigns these roles to
autoregressive pretraining for knowledge acquisition and diffusion post-training
for high-fidelity rendering.
Within this framework, we study the objective, representation, and scaling of knowledge acquisition and rendering.
Controlled comparisons identify autoregression as the stronger pretraining objective for downstream rendering, improving both learning efficiency and final generation
quality. We further find that AR-only generation quality does not necessarily correlate with final performance; semantic quality matters more. This motivates a
purely semantic tokenizer trained with language supervision alone, without an
image decoder or reconstruction loss. We establish compute-optimal scaling laws
for knowledge acquisition and rendering, and find that autoregressive pretraining
lowers the fitted asymptotic rendering loss compared with pixel diffusion models trained from scratch. Guided by the laws, we train a 3B-parameter text-to-image model with only 6,600 H100 GPU-hours, achieving 86 on GenEval and 87 on DPG-Bench and validating the proposed paradigm at scale.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Visual generation has advanced primarily through two modeling paradigms: autoregressive models predict discrete visual tokens ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Pang et al., 2024 ) , while latent diffusion models (LDMs) and pixel diffusion models (PDMs) denoise continuous signals ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) . They are typically compared as competing paradigms, asking which produces better images. Yet this comparison asks each paradigm to solve two distinct learning problems: acquiring high-level visual knowledge and rendering it into detailed images . We therefore argue that these problems need not favor the same objective, and look beyond their competition to uncover the synergy between autoregression and diffusion. We find that the two problems indeed favor different objectives: autoregression for visual knowledge acquisition and diffusion for rendering . This specialization gives rise to a natural pretraining–post-training paradigm , where autoregressive pretraining provides the foundation on which diffusion is post-trained for rendering. This mirrors modern language models, where broad knowledge is first acquired and subsequently adapted toward desired behaviors. At inference, the autoregressive rollout provides a structured visual representation that conditions diffusion, connecting the two learning processes. Across the evaluated protocols and compute budgets, this specialization consistently yields stronger generators, revealing the synergy between the two objectives. Specializing autoregression for knowledge acquisition changes what it should learn. In visual autoregressive models, the tokenizer defines the prediction target and therefore shapes the information the model is incentivized to capture. Conventional tokenizers preserve low-level appearance for image reconstruction. Once rendering is delegated to diffusion, however, the autoregressive representation no longer needs to support reconstruction or standalone image generation. Across different tokenizers, we find a striking dissociation: neither reconstruction quality nor AR-only generation quality determines post-training generation performance; semantic quality does. This motivates Semantic-LM , a semantic tokenizer trained through language supervision alone, without an image decoder or reconstruction loss. Visual tokenization thus shifts from preserving pixels for reconstruction to providing semantic learning targets for autoregressive knowledge acquisition. Separating knowledge acquisition from rendering introduces a new question for scaling visual generation: how should compute be allocated between the two stages? We establish scaling laws for autoregressive pretraining and diffusion post-training that characterize the effects of model size, data, and compute and guide compute-optimal allocation. These laws also reveal a broader benefit of autoregressive pretraining. At matched model and data scales, diffusion post-training achieves both lower loss and a lower fitted asymptotic rendering loss than PDM trained from scratch. This finding suggests that autoregressive pretraining improves the attainable performance of diffusion rendering beyond accelerating convergence speed. Given an available training budget of approximately 6,600 H100 GPU-hours, we use our scaling laws to select a roughly 3B-parameter model and allocate compute between pretraining and post-training. The resulting model achieves strong text-to-image generation (Fig. 1 ), reaching 0.86 on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) and 87.78 on DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . This performance is achieved with approximately 1/48 of the estimated training compute of Z-Image-Base ( Z-Image Team et al., 2025 ) , while attaining comparable DPG-Bench performance.

sections.heading: 2 Method
sections.text: As shown in Fig. 2 , our framework assigns visual knowledge acquisition and rendering to distinct learning objectives. During pretraining, a frozen visual tokenizer converts images into discrete tokens, which a text-conditioned autoregressive (AR) model learns to predict. We then freeze the AR backbone and add trainable pixel-diffusion modules that reuse its attention projections and representations for rendering. During post-training, the renderer conditions on tokens from ground-truth images; at inference, these are replaced by tokens generated autoregressively from the text prompt. Figure 2: Overview of our learning paradigm. Autoregressive pretraining acquires visual knowledge through discrete token prediction. The pretrained backbone is then frozen and augmented with diffusion modules that reuse its attention and representations to render high-fidelity images. This division of labor specializes autoregression for knowledge acquisition and diffusion for rendering.

sections.heading: 2.1 Autoregressive Pretraining for Knowledge Acquisition
sections.text: Autoregressive objective. Following RandAR ( Pang et al., 2024 ) , we sample a permutation π \pi over spatial positions and use position-instruction tokens 𝐨 \mathbf{o} to specify each prediction location. Only the AR parameters θ \theta are optimized. By defining the prediction targets, the tokenizer determines what information the model is trained to capture. Visual tokenizers. The visual tokenizer defines the prediction targets for AR pretraining and thus shapes the information the model learns. To examine which targets best support visual knowledge acquisition, we compare three tokenizers with different visual representations and training supervision (Fig. 3 ), including Recon , Semantic-Recon , and Semantic-LM . Figure 3: Training the three visual tokenizers. Recon and Semantic-Recon use image reconstruction supervision, whereas Semantic-LM learns its codebook through language modeling. • Recon. We use the pretrained reconstruction-based Emu3.5 tokenizer ( Cui et al., 2025 ) , which consists of an image encoder, an IBQ codebook ( Shi et al., 2025a ) , and an image decoder. • Semantic-Recon. We quantize features of a frozen Qwen2.5-VL vision encoder ( Bai et al., 2025 ) using an IBQ codebook. We train the codebook and a decoder with reconstruction supervision. • Semantic-LM. We use the same semantic visual representation but train the IBQ codebook through next-token prediction within a frozen Qwen2.5-VL model. This variant requires neither an image decoder nor a reconstruction loss. These variants let us examine two design choices. Comparing Recon with Semantic-Recon evaluates the benefit of using semantic representations for AR pretraining. Comparing Semantic-Recon with Semantic-LM tests whether reconstruction supervision is necessary for learning effective semantic tokens. All tokenizers remain frozen during generator training and are evaluated using the same protocol. We provide the tokenizer training details in Appendix A.1 .

sections.heading: 2.3 Scaling Methodology
sections.text: Separating knowledge acquisition from rendering introduces a resource allocation problem: given a fixed compute budget, how much should be assigned to each stage, and how should each stage balance model size and training data? We address these questions by fitting scaling laws for autoregressive pretraining and diffusion post-training. We also fit scaling law for a pixel-diffusion baseline trained from scratch to examine the benefits of autoregressive pretraining. Fitting objective-specific scaling laws. For each objective, we train a family of models across widths and depths and fit ℒ ^ ​ ( N , D ) = E + A ​ ( N N 0 ) − α + B ​ ( D D 0 ) − β , \widehat{\mathcal{L}}(N,D)=E+A\left(\frac{N}{N_{0}}\right)^{-\alpha}+B\left(\frac{D}{D_{0}}\right)^{-\beta}, (3) where N N is the number of trainable parameters, D D is the cumulative training-token count, and E E estimates the asymptotic loss under the fitted model. We fit autoregressive cross-entropy and diffusion velocity-MSE separately, using C = 6 ​ N ​ D C=6ND as a compute proxy. For diffusion post-training, this proxy excludes the frozen AR forward pass (Appendix A.8 ). We cross-check the parametric fits using training-curve envelopes and IsoFLOP analyses. To reduce optimization-related confounds, we tune training recipes that transfer across model sizes within each family. We also conduct an independent hyperparameter search for the from-scratch diffusion baseline. Appendices A.3 and A.6 describe hyperparameter transfer. Appendices A.4 and A.5 provide compute accounting and the full scaling protocols. Optimizing the learning paradigm through compute allocation. Within our two-stage framework, compute allocation determines the relative emphasis on knowledge acquisition and rendering. We parameterize this allocation by r = C post / ( C pre + C post ) r=C_{\mathrm{post}}/(C_{\mathrm{pre}}+C_{\mathrm{post}}) , so that different values of r r define different learning paradigm. To derive a scaling-guided allocation, we first minimize each stage’s fitted loss under the compute constraint C = 6 ​ N ​ D C=6ND . For each paired AR backbone and diffusion renderer, we then determine the data budget required to place each stage at its compute-optimal operating point. The resulting compute costs specify the allocation r r , which we examine across total budgets. This procedure translates the stage-specific scaling laws into a concrete training strategy without directly combining autoregressive and diffusion losses. We additionally compare the fitted asymptotic losses of diffusion post-training and pixel diffusion trained from scratch to assess potential benefits beyond faster convergence. Sec. 3.3 presents the results.

sections.heading: 3 Experiments
sections.text: Our experiments address three questions. First, does autoregressive pretraining lead to better image generation than diffusion-based training under comparable model sizes and image exposure? (Sec. 3.1 ) Second, should the visual tokens used for pretraining preserve image details or focus on semantic information? (Sec. 3.2 ) Third, how should model size, training data, and compute be allocated between knowledge acquisition and rendering? (Sec. 3.3 ) We then use these findings to guide the training of a larger text-to-image model and evaluate its generation quality (Sec. 3.4 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Autoregression or Diffusion for Visual Knowledge Acquisition?
sections.text: We assess visual knowledge acquisition through the quality of image generation after pixel-diffusion post-training. We compare latent diffusion and autoregression as pretraining objectives, followed by the same rendering architecture and post-training protocol. We denote these two-stage routes as LDM → \xrightarrow{} PDM and AR → \xrightarrow{} PDM . We also include pixel diffusion and latent diffusion as baselines. Training and Evaluation Setup. All four routes use approximately 400M parameters in the final generator and the same cumulative number of training image samples. Both two-stage routes combine a 250M-parameter pretrained backbone with 150M trainable rendering parameters. They also use semantic visual representations: AR uses our semantic tokenizer, while LDM pretraining uses SVG Autoencoder-P, a semantic tokenizer built on DINOv3 ( Shi et al., 2025b ; Siméoni et al., 2025 ) . The former produces discrete tokens, whereas the latter produces continuous representations. The direct LDM baseline uses the reconstruction-based FLUX.2 autoencoder ( Black Forest Labs, 2025 ) . We evaluate generation quality on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) and DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . Tab. 4 and Appendix A.2 provide the full training and evaluation protocols. Results. Autoregressive pretraining yields better generation quality after diffusion post-training than the evaluated LDM-pretraining pipeline. AR → \xrightarrow{} PDM reaches 64.8 on GenEval after 100k post-training updates, exceeding the score of PDM trained for 400k iterations (61.2). With further post-training, it reaches 65.5 on GenEval and 71.1 on DPG-Bench (Tab. 1 ). In contrast, direct LDM reaches 57.3 on GenEval, while LDM → \xrightarrow{} PDM achieves 56.6. These results indicate that splitting training into two stages alone is insufficient for generation. Under the evaluated settings, autoregression provides a more effective pretraining objective for subsequent pixel-diffusion rendering. sections.heading: 3.4 Validating the Learning Paradigm at Scale
sections.text: Finally, we evaluate whether the training recipe developed through our controlled experiments and scaling analysis remains effective at larger scale. Guided by the scaling laws in Sec. 3.3 , we train a roughly 3B-parameter text-to-image generator using approximately 6,600 H100 GPU-hours. We evaluate compositional accuracy and text–image alignment on GenEval and DPG-Bench, with results reported in Tab. 3 . Category-level scores for HiDream-I1-Full, PixNerd, and SeFi-Image-5B are taken from their original reports ( Cai et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; SeFi Team, 2026 ) . For BLIP3o-4B, BLIP3o-NEXT SFT, and i1, we use the aggregate scores reported by Zeng et al. (2026) , as category-level scores are unavailable under that evaluation. Our model achieves 0.86 on GenEval and 87.78 on DPG-Bench using the evaluation protocol in Appendix A.9 , which includes prompt rewriting and selection over fixed evaluation seeds. Among the baselines in Tab. 3 , only Qwen-Image and Seedream 3.0 report higher DPG-Bench scores. Our GenEval score is also close to those of Qwen-Image and BLIP3o-NEXT SFT (both 0.87) and SeFi-Image-5B (0.88). These results support the practical effectiveness of our training recipe at larger scale. Comparisons across systems remain approximate because text encoders, training data, and evaluation settings differ. The results demonstrate competitive generation quality within the stated training budget, without establishing that the compute allocation is optimal.

sections.heading: 4 Related Work
sections.text: Diffusion-based visual generation. Diffusion models have evolved from pixel-space denoising ( Ho et al., 2020 ) to latent diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , transformer backbones ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) , and flow-based objectives ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) , underpinning modern text-to-image systems ( Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Black Forest Labs, 2025 ; Z-Image Team et al., 2025 ; Cai et al., 2025 ) . Recent work shows that representation quality matters beyond reconstruction fidelity ( Skorokhodov et al., 2025 ; Yao et al., 2025 ) , motivating semantically enriched tokenizers and diffusion representations ( Chen et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2025b ; Tong et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Leng et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2025 ; SeFi Team, 2026 ) . These approaches make diffusion representations more semantic, but semantic learning remains coupled to reconstruction or diffusion itself. We instead separate knowledge acquisition from rendering: autoregressive pretraining learns the semantic representation consumed by the renderer, while diffusion is specialized for rendering it into pixels. This separation further enables Semantic-LM, trained purely through language supervision without an image decoder or reconstruction loss. Autoregressive visual generation. Autoregressive image models predict learned visual tokens ( Van Den Oord et al., 2017 ; Esser et al., 2021 ; Yu et al., 2023 ; Shi et al., 2025a ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) using raster, next-scale, or randomized prediction ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Pang et al., 2024 ) . Tokenizer design is central to this paradigm ( Yu et al., 2023 ) , with recent work incorporating foundation-model representations or semantic supervision ( Zheng et al., 2025a ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . In these approaches, autoregression remains part of image generation, so its representation must support visual synthesis. We instead specialize autoregression for knowledge acquisition and delegate rendering to diffusion, freeing its prediction targets from reconstruction or AR-only generation. Combining autoregression and diffusion. Several works combine autoregressive and diffusion modeling within a single generative framework. MAR ( Li et al., 2024 ) uses diffusion as the conditional distribution within continuous-token autoregression, while Transfusion ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) applies autoregressive and diffusion objectives to different modalities in a shared model. More closely related, concurrent VoT ( Sun et al., 2026 ) predicts semantic visual tokens before diffusion rendering to extend pretrained VLMs toward unified model. Our distinction is not in how the two objectives are combined, but in what they are asked to learn. We assign autoregression to visual knowledge acquisition during pretraining and introduce diffusion only afterward for rendering, enabling the two roles to be optimized and scaled separately. Scaling laws for generative models. Scaling laws characterize model–data–compute tradeoffs and compute-optimal training ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Henighan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) , while transferable parameterizations enable consistent optimization across scale ( Yang et al., 2022 ; Dey et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025c ) . Recent work extends scaling analysis to visual diffusion ( Ge et al., 2026 ) . Whereas prior studies primarily scale a single learning objective, we study cross-objective allocation between knowledge acquisition and rendering.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We propose a visual generation paradigm that separates knowledge acquisition from rendering: autoregressive pretraining learns visual knowledge, and diffusion renders it into pixels. Through controlled experiments and scaling analysis, we identify three advantages of this approach. First, semantic tokens provide effective pretraining targets without requiring image reconstruction or standalone AR generation. Second, stage-specific scaling laws guide compute allocation, while the lower fitted asymptotic rendering loss suggests benefits of the pretrained pipeline beyond faster convergence. Third, these findings translate into a compute-efficient text-to-image generator that achieves 0.86 on GenEval and 87.78 on DPG-Bench with approximately 6,600 H100 GPU-hours of training. Together, our results support a practical approach to visual generation that tailors the learning objective, representation, and compute budget to each stage.

sections.text: We provide training and evaluation details for the controlled comparisons, hyperparameter studies, and scaling experiments.

sections.heading: A.1 Semantic Tokenizer Training
sections.text: We train two semantic tokenizers to study the role of codebook supervision: Semantic-Recon uses image reconstruction, whereas Semantic-LM uses language modeling. Both quantize post-merger features from the frozen Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct visual encoder using an IBQ codebook ( Shi et al., 2025a ) . Tokenizer training is separate from the AR-pretraining and diffusion-post-training budgets reported in Appendix A.2 ; the resulting tokenizers remain frozen throughout generator training.

sections.heading: Shared configuration.
sections.text: The IBQ codebook contains 131,072 entries with code dimension 256 and quantization temperature 0.25. Both tokenizers use an entropy regularization coefficient of 0.05 and a global batch size of 256. The optimizer uses β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 , ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} , and weight decay 0.01; gradients are clipped at norm 1. We linearly warm up the learning rate to 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} over 10,000 updates, then apply cosine decay with a minimum learning rate of 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} . Training uses three native-resolution tiers with image areas near 256 2 256^{2} , 512 2 512^{2} , and 1024 2 1024^{2} pixels and random aspect ratios. We sample these tiers in a 4:2:1 ratio by number of examples. This sample ratio is distinct from the token quotas used for generator training.

sections.heading: Semantic-Recon.
sections.text: An IBQ codebook quantizes the frozen post-merger visual features, and a transformer decoder reconstructs the input image from the quantized representation. The decoder has 12 layers, hidden width 768, and 12 attention heads. We train the codebook and decoder on in-house training data for 80,000 updates. The objective combines image reconstruction, VGG-based LPIPS perceptual supervision, and quantization loss, with respective weights 1, 0.5, and 1, together with the entropy regularizer specified above. The pretrained visual feature extractor remains frozen. We maintain an exponential moving average of the trainable parameters with decay 0.9999 and a 2,000-update warmup.

sections.heading: Semantic-LM.
sections.text: We freeze Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct, including its visual feature extractor and language model, and train only the IBQ codebook. Quantized visual features condition the frozen language model, and next-token cross-entropy on the supervised text targets provides the codebook’s training signal. This language-modeling objective is not restricted to image captions. We train for 40,000 updates on the 200B version of DataComp-VLM ( Farina et al., 2026 ) , using the shared optimization and resolution settings above. The objective combines language-modeling cross-entropy with entropy regularization at weight 0.05. No image decoder or image reconstruction loss is used.

sections.heading: Model capacity.
sections.text: For the direct-pixel and AR controls, we match the total parameter count of the final generators at approximately 400M total parameters. The PDM has width 1408, 16 layers, 11 attention heads with head dimension 128, and feed-forward hidden dimension 3840. The AR backbone uses the same width, attention configuration, and feed-forward dimension, but only eight layers. Diffusion post-training adds randomly initialized rendering modules, including separate diffusion feed-forward layers, while keeping the AR parameters frozen. The AR-pretraining backbone has approximately 250M parameters, and the rendering modules add approximately 150M, giving a final generator of approximately 400M that matches the PDM. This matched size refers to the final generator, not to the number of parameters used during pretraining. Total parameter counts include the frozen AR backbone and trainable rendering modules, count shared weights once, and exclude external frozen text encoders and tokenizers.

sections.heading: Tokenizer controls.
sections.text: For the comparisons among Recon, Semantic-Recon, and Semantic-LM, the tokenizer is the only experimental variable. All three use the same generator architecture, training images and captions, preprocessing, sample order, resolution curriculum, token budget, and stage durations. We also align code-embedding initialization, optimization, text conditioning, checkpoint selection, and generation evaluation. Each tokenizer remains frozen during generator training. sections.heading: Initialization and transfer rules.
sections.text: Our reference dimensions are width W 0 = 512 W_{0}=512 , depth L 0 = 4 L_{0}=4 , and FFN hidden dimension F 0 = 1536 F_{0}=1536 . Define m W = W / W 0 m_{W}=W/W_{0} and m L = L / L 0 m_{L}=L/L_{0} . We fix the base initialization scale at s 0 = 0.02 s_{0}=0.02 throughout the sweep. Attention and FFN matrices use zero-mean truncated-normal initialization with scale s 0 / m W s_{0}/\sqrt{m_{W}} . The width-to-width text projection uses a normal distribution with the same scale. Input/output code projections, the first text projection, and position-instruction token embeddings use normal initialization with scale s 0 s_{0} ; normalization gains start at one and the output bias at zero. The tied code table is initialized from the frozen tokenizer’s codebook values, then trained as part of the AR model. Following CompleteP-style depth scaling with exponent one, both the attention and FFN residual updates are multiplied by m L − 1 m_{L}^{-1} , and the hidden states entering the factorized readout are scaled by m W − 1 m_{W}^{-1} . For a hidden matrix, let m p m_{p} be its fan-in multiplier: m p = m W m_{p}=m_{W} except for the FFN down projection, where m p = F / F 0 m_{p}=F/F_{0} . sections.heading: Final-model training.
sections.text: The large-scale AR backbone has width 2304 and 27 layers. It uses frozen Qwen3-4B text features from layers 9, 18, and 27, concatenated to 7680 dimensions; feature extraction stops at layer 27 and uses BF16. AR pretraining uses a global batch size of 2048 and a caption mixture of 70% flattened long captions and 30% canonical structured captions. The 150k-update AR curriculum uses 50k updates at the 256-resolution tier, ramps toward a 50/25/25 mixture of the 256/512/1024 tiers over the next 50k, and holds that mixture for the last 50k. These proportions count examples within the global batch. This final-model recipe is separate from the controlled comparisons in Tab. 2 . We then freeze the AR backbone and train the diffusion modules for 100,000 updates with global batch size 512. Diffusion uses four times as many visual target tokens per image as AR pretraining, so we reduce its image batch size by a factor of four. This balances visual-target throughput per update at a matched resolution. Guided by the prescribed 3 : 2 3{:}2 stage allocation, we use a matching ratio of pretraining to post-training updates. Post-training follows the diffusion resolution curriculum, preserving its resolution proportions while reducing each resolution-specific batch size proportionally to give global batch size 512. We use AdamW with weight decay 0.01 and base learning rate 8 × 10 − 4 8\times 10^{-4} , selected by the post-training learning-rate search in Appendix A.5 .

sections.heading: Training cost.
sections.text: The total training budget is approximately 6,600 H100 GPU-hours. Following the prescribed 3 : 2 3{:}2 allocation, the nominal stage budgets are approximately 3,960 GPU-hours for AR pretraining and 2,640 GPU-hours for diffusion post-training. These are budget allocations rather than separate measurements of stage runtime.

sections.heading: Evaluation sampling.
sections.text: We use an exponential moving average (EMA) of the trainable diffusion parameters, with decay 0.9999 starting at update 20,000; the frozen AR parameters remain unchanged. We set AR classifier-free guidance (CFG) to 3 and use a 50-step Euler sampler for diffusion, with AR-conditioning CFG 3 and text-conditioning CFG 4. GenEval uses 553 prompts with one image per prompt and seed 42; DPG-Bench uses 1,065 prompts with four images per prompt and seeds 42–45. We use LLM-assisted prompt rewriting and select prompt variants using evaluation scores under fixed seeds.

sections.heading: A.10 Discussion: Semantic inference and rendering in frontier models.
sections.text: Our results suggest a broader interpretation of the separation between knowledge acquisition and rendering. We suspect that frontier visual generators ( OpenAI, 2026 ; Ideogram, ; Reve, 2026 ) increasingly perform substantial semantic inference before committing to pixel generation. An autoregressive process can expand a user request into a richer specification through text or visual tokens, structured representations, retrieved information, or agentic interaction. Prompt rewriting and long textual rollouts are simple instances of this principle ( Chen et al., 2026 ) : additional context progressively specifies the desired image and reduces the ambiguity left to the renderer. Under this view, the role of autoregression is not necessarily to produce an image that can already be decoded, but to resolve what should be rendered; diffusion can then focus on realizing this specification in pixels. Semantic-LM admits a similar interpretation. Its discrete visual tokens are trained through language supervision and need not reconstruct or directly generate an image. They can instead be viewed as a compressed semantic state between inference and rendering. In this sense, a semantic visual rollout and a long textual rollout may serve related purposes: both enrich the renderer’s conditioning context, but visual tokens may encode the relevant information more compactly and in a spatially grounded form. This perspective also raises a question not resolved by our current experiments. Semantic-Recon retains reconstruction-oriented visual information, whereas Semantic-LM more directly aligns its representation with language semantics. Without explicit textual rollouts, our results do not determine which interface is preferable when a generator already has access to rich language or agentic context. We suspect that Semantic-LM may be particularly compatible with such inference, while Semantic-Recon may preserve complementary visual information. Understanding how textual, visual, structured, and agentic representations should interact—and how much uncertainty each should resolve before rendering—is an important direction for future visual generation systems. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.37626v1 [cs.CV] 27 Oct 2026 Know, then Draw: A New Learning Paradigm for Visual Generation Yucheng Mao Affiliation: University of California, San Diego Affiliation: Adobe Research Chongjian Ge Affiliation: Adobe Research Zhuowen Tu Affiliation: University of California, San Diego Hao Tan Affiliation: Adobe Research Hanwen Jiang Affiliation: Adobe Research Abstract Visual generation requires both high-level semantic knowledge and fine-grained pixel details. We propose a learning paradigm that assigns these roles to autoregressive pretraining for knowledge acquisition and diffusion post-training for high-fidelity rendering. Within this framework, we study the objective, representation, and scaling of knowledge acquisition and rendering. Controlled comparisons identify autoregression as the stronger pretraining objective for downstream rendering, improving both learning efficiency and final generation quality. We further find that AR-only generation quality does not necessarily correlate with final performance; semantic quality matters more. This motivates a purely semantic tokenizer trained with language supervision alone, without an image decoder or reconstruction loss. We establish compute-optimal scaling laws for knowledge acquisition and rendering, and find that autoregressive pretraining lowers the fitted asymptotic rendering loss compared with pixel diffusion models trained from scratch. Guided by the laws, we train a 3B-parameter text-to-image model with only 6,600 H100 GPU-hours, achieving 86 on GenEval and 87 on DPG-Bench and validating the proposed paradigm at scale. Figure 1: Strong visual generation with compute-efficient training. Left : DPG-Bench versus training compute; marker size denotes model size. Our 3B model achieves competitive performance with only 6,600 H100 GPU-hours ( 48 × 48\times less than Z-Image-Base). Right : Text-to-Image generated samples. 1 Introduction Visual generation has advanced primarily through two modeling paradigms: autoregressive models predict discrete visual tokens ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Pang et al., 2024 ) , while latent diffusion models (LDMs) and pixel diffusion models (PDMs) denoise continuous signals ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) . They are typically compared as competing paradigms, asking which produces better images. Yet this comparison asks each paradigm to solve two distinct learning problems: acquiring high-level visual knowledge and rendering it into detailed images . We therefore argue that these problems need not favor the same objective, and look beyond their competition to uncover the synergy between autoregression and diffusion. We find that the two problems indeed favor different objectives: autoregression for visual knowledge acquisition and diffusion for rendering . This specialization gives rise to a natural pretraining–post-training paradigm , where autoregressive pretraining provides the foundation on which diffusion is post-trained for rendering. This mirrors modern language models, where broad knowledge is first acquired and subsequently adapted toward desired behaviors. At inference, the autoregressive rollout provides a structured visual representation that conditions diffusion, connecting the two learning processes. Across the evaluated protocols and compute budgets, this specialization consistently yields stronger generators, revealing the synergy between the two objectives. Specializing autoregression for knowledge acquisition changes what it should learn. In visual autoregressive models, the tokenizer defines the prediction target and therefore shapes the information the model is incentivized to capture. Conventional tokenizers preserve low-level appearance for image reconstruction. Once rendering is delegated to diffusion, however, the autoregressive representation no longer needs to support reconstruction or standalone image generation. Across different tokenizers, we find a striking dissociation: neither reconstruction quality nor AR-only generation quality determines post-training generation performance; semantic quality does. This motivates Semantic-LM , a semantic tokenizer trained through language supervision alone, without an image decoder or reconstruction loss. Visual tokenization thus shifts from preserving pixels for reconstruction to providing semantic learning targets for autoregressive knowledge acquisition. Separating knowledge acquisition from rendering introduces a new question for scaling visual generation: how should compute be allocated between the two stages? We establish scaling laws for autoregressive pretraining and diffusion post-training that characterize the effects of model size, data, and compute and guide compute-optimal allocation. These laws also reveal a broader benefit of autoregressive pretraining. At matched model and data scales, diffusion post-training achieves both lower loss and a lower fitted asymptotic rendering loss than PDM trained from scratch. This finding suggests that autoregressive pretraining improves the attainable performance of diffusion rendering beyond accelerating convergence speed. Given an available training budget of approximately 6,600 H100 GPU-hours, we use our scaling laws to select a roughly 3B-parameter model and allocate compute between pretraining and post-training. The resulting model achieves strong text-to-image generation (Fig. 1 ), reaching 0.86 on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) and 87.78 on DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . This performance is achieved with approximately 1/48 of the estimated training compute of Z-Image-Base ( Z-Image Team et al., 2025 ) , while attaining comparable DPG-Bench performance. 2 Method As shown in Fig. 2 , our framework assigns visual knowledge acquisition and rendering to distinct learning objectives. During pretraining, a frozen visual tokenizer converts images into discrete tokens, which a text-conditioned autoregressive (AR) model learns to predict. We then freeze the AR backbone and add trainable pixel-diffusion modules that reuse its attention projections and representations for rendering. During post-training, the renderer conditions on tokens from ground-truth images; at inference, these are replaced by tokens generated autoregressively from the text prompt. Figure 2: Overview of our learning paradigm. Autoregressive pretraining acquires visual knowledge through discrete token prediction. The pretrained backbone is then frozen and augmented with diffusion modules that reuse its attention and representations to render high-fidelity images. This division of labor specializes autoregression for knowledge acquisition and diffusion for rendering. 2.1 Autoregressive Pretraining for Knowledge Acquisition Autoregressive objective. The visual tokenizer defines the prediction targets for AR pretraining and thus shapes the information the model learns. At inference, the AR model generates visual tokens from the text prompt, and these tokens condition the renderer. 2.3 Scaling Methodology Separating knowledge acquisition from rendering introduces a resource allocation problem: given a fixed compute budget, how much should be assigned to each stage, and how should each stage balance model size and training data? We address these questions by fitting scaling laws for autoregressive pretraining and diffusion post-training. We also fit scaling law for a pixel-diffusion baseline trained from scratch to examine the benefits of autoregressive pretraining. Fitting objective-specific scaling laws. For each objective, we train a family of models across widths and depths and fit ℒ ^ ​ ( N , D ) = E + A ​ ( N N 0 ) − α + B ​ ( D D 0 ) − β , \widehat{\mathcal{L}}(N,D)=E+A\left(\frac{N}{N_{0}}\right)^{-\alpha}+B\left(\frac{D}{D_{0}}\right)^{-\beta}, (3) where N N is the number of trainable parameters, D D is the cumulative training-token count, and E E estimates the asymptotic loss under the fitted model. We fit autoregressive cross-entropy and diffusion velocity-MSE separately, using C = 6 ​ N ​ D C=6ND as a compute proxy. For diffusion post-training, this proxy excludes the frozen AR forward pass (Appendix A.8 ). We cross-check the parametric fits using training-curve envelopes and IsoFLOP analyses. To reduce optimization-related confounds, we tune training recipes that transfer across model sizes within each family. We also conduct an independent hyperparameter search for the from-scratch diffusion baseline. Appendices A.3 and A.6 describe hyperparameter transfer. Appendices A.4 and A.5 provide compute accounting and the full scaling protocols. Optimizing the learning paradigm through compute allocation. Within our two-stage framework, compute allocation determines the relative emphasis on knowledge acquisition and rendering. We parameterize this allocation by r = C post / ( C pre + C post ) r=C_{\mathrm{post}}/(C_{\mathrm{pre}}+C_{\mathrm{post}}) , so that different values of r r define different learning paradigm. To derive a scaling-guided allocation, we first minimize each stage’s fitted loss under the compute constraint C = 6 ​ N ​ D C=6ND . For each paired AR backbone and diffusion renderer, we then determine the data budget required to place each stage at its compute-optimal operating point. The resulting compute costs specify the allocation r r , which we examine across total budgets. This procedure translates the stage-specific scaling laws into a concrete training strategy without directly combining autoregressive and diffusion losses. We additionally compare the fitted asymptotic losses of diffusion post-training and pixel diffusion trained from scratch to assess potential benefits beyond faster convergence. Sec. 3.3 presents the results. 3 Experiments Our experiments address three questions. First, does autoregressive pretraining lead to better image generation than diffusion-based training under comparable model sizes and image exposure? (Sec. 3.1 ) Second, should the visual tokens used for pretraining preserve image details or focus on semantic information? (Sec. 3.2 ) Third, how should model size, training data, and compute be allocated between knowledge acquisition and rendering? (Sec. 3.3 ) We then use these findings to guide the training of a larger text-to-image model and evaluate its generation quality (Sec. 3.4 ). 3.1 Autoregression or Diffusion for Visual Knowledge Acquisition? We assess visual knowledge acquisition through the quality of image generation after pixel-diffusion post-training. We compare latent diffusion and autoregression as pretraining objectives, followed by the same rendering architecture and post-training protocol. We denote these two-stage routes as LDM → \xrightarrow{} PDM and AR → \xrightarrow{} PDM . We also include pixel diffusion and latent diffusion as baselines. Training and Evaluation Setup. All four routes use approximately 400M parameters in the final generator and the same cumulative number of training image samples. Both two-stage routes combine a 250M-parameter pretrained backbone with 150M trainable rendering parameters. They also use semantic visual representations: AR uses our semantic tokenizer, while LDM pretraining uses SVG Autoencoder-P, a semantic tokenizer built on DINOv3 ( Shi et al., 2025b ; Siméoni et al., 2025 ) . The former produces discrete tokens, whereas the latter produces continuous representations. The direct LDM baseline uses the reconstruction-based FLUX.2 autoencoder ( Black Forest Labs, 2025 ) . We evaluate generation quality on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) and DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . Tab. 4 and Appendix A.2 provide the full training and evaluation protocols. Results. Autoregressive pretraining yields better generation quality after diffusion post-training than the evaluated LDM-pretraining pipeline. These results indicate that splitting training into two stages alone is insufficient for generation. Under the evaluated settings, autoregression provides a more effective pretraining objective for subsequent pixel-diffusion rendering. Diffusion models have evolved from pixel-space denoising ( Ho et al., 2020 ) to latent diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , transformer backbones ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) , and flow-based objectives ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) , underpinning modern text-to-image systems ( Black Forest Labs, 2024 ; Black Forest Labs, 2025 ; Z-Image Team et al., 2025 ; Cai et al., 2025 ) . Recent work shows that representation quality matters beyond reconstruction fidelity ( Skorokhodov et al., 2025 ; Yao et al., 2025 ) , motivating semantically enriched tokenizers and diffusion representations ( Chen et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2025b ; Tong et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Leng et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2025 ; SeFi Team, 2026 ) . These approaches make diffusion representations more semantic, but semantic learning remains coupled to reconstruction or diffusion itself. We instead separate knowledge acquisition from rendering: autoregressive pretraining learns the semantic representation consumed by the renderer, while diffusion is specialized for rendering it into pixels. This separation further enables Semantic-LM, trained purely through language supervision without an image decoder or reconstruction loss. Autoregressive visual generation. Autoregressive image models predict learned visual tokens ( Van Den Oord et al., 2017 ; Esser et al., 2021 ; Yu et al., 2023 ; Shi et al., 2025a ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) using raster, next-scale, or randomized prediction ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Pang et al., 2024 ) . Tokenizer design is central to this paradigm ( Yu et al., 2023 ) , with recent work incorporating foundation-model representations or semantic supervision ( Zheng et al., 2025a ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . In these approaches, autoregression remains part of image generation, so its representation must support visual synthesis. We instead specialize autoregression for knowledge acquisition and delegate rendering to diffusion, freeing its prediction targets from reconstruction or AR-only generation. Combining autoregression and diffusion. Several works combine autoregressive and diffusion modeling within a single generative framework. MAR ( Li et al., 2024 ) uses diffusion as the conditional distribution within continuous-token autoregression, while Transfusion ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) applies autoregressive and diffusion objectives to different modalities in a shared model. More closely related, concurrent VoT ( Sun et al., 2026 ) predicts semantic visual tokens before diffusion rendering to extend pretrained VLMs toward unified model. Our distinction is not in how the two objectives are combined, but in what they are asked to learn. We assign autoregression to visual knowledge acquisition during pretraining and introduce diffusion only afterward for rendering, enabling the two roles to be optimized and scaled separately. Scaling laws for generative models. Scaling laws characterize model–data–compute tradeoffs and compute-optimal training ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Henighan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) , while transferable parameterizations enable consistent optimization across scale ( Yang et al., 2022 ; Dey et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025c ) . Recent work extends scaling analysis to visual diffusion ( Ge et al., 2026 ) . Whereas prior studies primarily scale a single learning objective, we study cross-objective allocation between knowledge acquisition and rendering. 5 Conclusion We propose a visual generation paradigm that separates knowledge acquisition from rendering: autoregressive pretraining learns visual knowledge, and diffusion renders it into pixels. Through controlled experiments and scaling analysis, we identify three advantages of this approach. First, semantic tokens provide effective pretraining targets without requiring image reconstruction or standalone AR generation. Second, stage-specific scaling laws guide compute allocation, while the lower fitted asymptotic rendering loss suggests benefits of the pretrained pipeline beyond faster convergence. Third, these findings translate into a compute-efficient text-to-image generator that achieves 0.86 on GenEval and 87.78 on DPG-Bench with approximately 6,600 H100 GPU-hours of training. Together, our results support a practical approach to visual generation that tailors the learning objective, representation, and compute budget to each stage. References Bai et al. (2025) S. Bai, K.
